I am a sound engineer on a live music show, and Saturday is the day that matters. We get to the studio at noon and set up the stage: twelve microphones, two drum kits and a piano. At four, we have the sound check. Each band plays one song, and we play it back in the control room to check the balance. Last week, one singer said her voice was too loud in her ear monitor, so I turned it down, and she was happy. Then, one hour before we went live, a wireless microphone broke down. There was no time to repair it, so we went over the plan again and gave her a spare one. The show is live, so we can't put anything off. If something goes wrong during the show, we carry on, and we sort it out in the break. Nobody at home ever knows.

People always ask me how I come up with ideas for songs. Honestly, it is not magic. It is a system. Every morning, I record one minute of anything: a melody, a beat, a sentence. I don't judge it. I just save it and carry on with my day. On Fridays, I go over everything I recorded that week. I play each idea back once, and most of them are terrible. That's fine. Maybe one is interesting, and I keep that one. My biggest problem was always putting things off. I used to say, I will start the song next week, and next week never came. Now I have a rule. If an idea is good, I work on it the same day, even for ten minutes. And when a song doesn't work, I don't throw it away. I take it back to voice and guitar, and very often it comes back to life.

The assistant engineer set up the microphones before the band arrived. The singer asked the engineer to turn the band down. During the coffee break, the guitarist came up with a new intro. In the middle of the third take, the old mixing desk broke down. The engineer went over every connection and sorted it out. The producer put the vocal off until Thursday.
